newsitem.title: INDONESIA: U.S. official visits Indonesia detainees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official visits Indonesia detainees.

text.p: A senior U.S. diplomat met two Indonesians who were detained during a crackdown in the aftermath of Jakarta's July riots, the official said on Friday.

U.S. Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Winston Lord, visiting Jakarta to inquire into Indonesia's human rights record, said he met independent labour leader Muchtar Pakpahan and activist Budiman Sudjatmiko in their cells.
The brief meetings with the detainees on Friday were at the invitation of Attorney-General Singgih, Lord said.
The two were charged with subversion in connection with riots in Jakarta on July 27, a crime punishable by death.
"There was not much time to spend with either individual," Lord told a news conference.

"It was mostly a matter of entering into where they are now residing, shaking hands and leaving. I was glad to have the opportunity to do that and it symbolises our interest in recent events." He did not comment on their condition.

The United States has expressed concern at the crackdown in Indonesia, saying it fears that those detained were not given an opportunity for due process and that political opponents of the government are being charged with criminal offences.

Lord said he met senior Indonesian officials, the national human rights commission, representatives of non-governmental organisations and community leaders for their reactions to the political dissent preceding the riots and the subsequent crackdown.
"I've come away with a better understanding of all points of view here and I would like to reflect on what I've heard," he said. "I don't think it's appropriate for me to pass instant judgments."

The riots, in which at least five people died and scores of buildings and vehicles were set ablaze, erupted after police raided the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) to evict supporters of ousted party head Megawati Sukarnoputri.

Megawati, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno, had become a symbol of dissent after she was ousted by a government-backed faction of the PDI in June. She has not been arrested but has undergone three sessions of questioning by the police and the attorney-general's office.
The government took more than 200 people into custody after the riots. It has charged nine with subversion and some 120 are still in jail and are likely to be charged with rioting.

Lord said Washington was prepared to go ahead with selling F-16 jet fighters to Indonesia, a sale that was delayed after members of the U.S. Congress expressed concern at Jakarta's human rights record in the wake of the riots.

"The administration has made it clear that we intend to go ahead with that sale, as early as January," Lord said. "We believe that Indonesia has legitimate self-defence needs. However, we do feel that it would be useful to have further consultations with Congress."
